title: Silent Teacher: Five reasons I model without talking
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton defends Silent Teacher, the practice of modelling a whole worked example in silence at the start of the I Do phase, against the obvious objection from the Modality Effect. Drawing on hundreds of lessons observed since his 2018 book, he gives five reasons it works: it focuses attention, removes the noise that talk breeds, heightens the power of gestures, prompts low-stakes principled and predictive self-explanation, and gives students a representation of the whole process before it is decomposed. He is equally clear that silence alone is not enough, and describes following it with narration plus checks for listening using cold call and call and respond. The piece ends with candid advice that it is a tool, not a rule, and may go awkwardly at first.
points: Silent modelling creates a clear cue for focus and makes any talking an obvious breach of expectations, which tackles the way noise begets noise in worked examples.
Pausing and tapping the head cues students to silently self-explain what has just happened and what comes next, with no pressure to answer aloud.
Following Pam Grossman's representation, decomposition, approximation sequence, Silent Teacher supplies the whole-process view that line-by-line explanation withholds.
Silent Teacher is only the first stage: narration with cold call and call-and-respond checks for listening must follow, then checks for understanding in the We Do.
Teachers should explain the purpose to students, choose a simple first example, and treat the technique as optional rather than constant.
quotes: This is where the teacher begins the I Do phase of a worked example by modelling the entire process in silence.

This collective focus will not happen right away with all classes. It is important to explain the purpose and expectations for behaviour during Silent Teacher, and hold students to account if they do not meet those expectations.
I watch many teachers deliver many worked examples, and one thing I have noticed is that the more the teacher talks, the greater the noise level in the room during that modelling.
Every time I pause, this is your cue to think: What have I just done, and what do you think I will do next.

The stakes are important here. Self-explaining is not having to explain what is going on to your partner or the teacher. It is a moment of silent self-reflection - an opportunity to take the first crucial steps in piecing together a new idea without any pressure.
I would explain each step of the process, often line-by-line. The problem is that students have not seen the bigger picture - they have no sense of where each of these steps is leading.

If the I Do started and finished with Silent Teacher it would be rubbish. We have not added the crucial verbal explanations needed to illustrate and illuminate what we have demonstrated visually. We also have zero evidence anyone has been paying attention, let alone has understood.
